source_title: PSL TREC 2024 report (Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
source_quote: Shoshone country included all the land north of the Yampa River, North Park, and the mountains to the Front Range north of what is now Rocky Mountain National Park.
notes: Quote is in the book, attributed to J. Donald Hughes via a Peter Faris article (secondary-of-secondary). Not checked against Hughes or Faris. Partial primary support only: 1863 Fort Bridger Art. 4 (Kappler II) names North Park ('Buffalo House') and the Yampah River as the Shoshone east and south limits as described by the Shoshone themselves. Would be settled by Hughes, American Indians in Colorado, and the Faris article.

source_title: PSL TREC 2024 report (Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
source_quote: range from the waters of Wind river [sic] or lati- tude 43° 30’ on the north and from the South Pass to the headwaters of the North Platte on the east
notes: Book quote confirmed in PSL text; original Lander 1859 report not reached. Settle with F.W. Lander's report on the Eastern Snakes (Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs 1859, or Sen. Ex. Doc. 42, 36th Cong., 1st Sess.). Consistent in general terms with 1863 Art. 4 (Wind River Mountains east, Yampah south).

source_title: Treaty of Fort Laramie with Sioux, etc., Sept. 17, 1851 (Kappler II)
source_quote: the Sioux or Dahcotahs , Cheyennes , Arrapahoes , Crows , Assina- boines , Gros- Ventre Mandans , and Arrickaras , parties of the second part
corrected_instrument_cite: Treaty of Fort Laramie, Sept. 17, 1851, Kappler II 594 (1904 ed.); 11 Stat. 749 as cited by Kappler
notes: Primary text lists the parties and Shoshone are not among them, confirming non-party status. The Superintendent's explanation quoted in PSL ('not considered ... as embraced by his instructions') was not checked against D.D. Mitchell's 1851 report (Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs 1851). Cheyenne killing and covering-the-bodies detail is book only.

source_title: Treaty of Fort Laramie, 1851, Art. 2 (Kappler II)
source_quote: The aforesaid nations do hereby recognize the right of the United States Government to establish roads, military and other posts, within their respective territories.
notes: Facts underneath confirmed: Art. 2 binds only 'the aforesaid nations' and the Shoshone were not among them. The conclusion that routes through Shoshone country had no treaty basis until 1863 is the PSL author's legal argument. Note the 1863 Fort Bridger treaty Arts. 2-3 later consented to existing and future routes, telegraph, stage lines and railway.

source_title: Treaty with the Eastern Band Shoshoni and Bannock, July 3, 1868
source_quote: rights in and to any portion of the territory of the United States, except such as is embraced within the limits
corrected_summary: The PSL author asserts land in present Colorado still belongs to the Shoshone. As a matter of treaty text, Art. II of the 1868 Fort Bridger treaty relinquished all title, claims or rights to any territory outside the Wind River reservation, which includes any Colorado lands described in 1863. The 1863 treaty did not cede land, and the Supreme Court held in 1945 that the 1863 Shoshone treaties did not recognize Indian title. Map this only as the author's claim, not as unceded land.
notes: Advocacy claim by the PSL author with no legal authority cited. The relinquishment is general, not Colorado-specific; whether compensation for that relinquishment was adequate is a separate question (see Shoshone ICC claims).

source_title: PSL TREC 2024 report (Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
source_quote: The path for the railroad was determined through Shoshone and other tribal lands without permission or a treaty, and over ten years before the Treaty of 1863.
notes: Survey history (Stansbury 1849-50; Pacific Railroad Surveys under the Army appropriation of March 3, 1853) is well documented generally, but the specific claims (10,000 copies printed; surveys spurred rushes) were not checked against the survey volumes or the 1855 printing resolution. 'Illegal mapping' is the author's characterization; no treaty barred surveying. Settle with Reports of Explorations and Surveys vol. II (1855) and the Feb. 1855 printing resolution.

source_title: Pacific Telegraph Act, June 16, 1860
source_quote: one quarter-section of land, such stations not to exceed one in fifteen miles
corrected_summary: The Pacific Telegraph Act was approved June 16, 1860 (not June 15). It let the contractor use 'unoccupied public lands of the United States' for right of way and repair stations of up to one quarter-section, about one per fifteen miles. It did not grant land outright. The line crossed Shoshone country in 1861 with no Shoshone treaty; the 1863 Fort Bridger treaty Art. 3 then agreed the existing telegraph might continue.
notes: Act text: permission 'to use until the end of the said term, such unoccupied public lands'. So 'granted a quarter-section per 15 miles' overstates: it was a use permission for stations, not a grant.

source_title: Shoshone Indians v. United States
source_quote: only secure freedom from molestation for the routes of travel
corrected_summary: The Supreme Court (Shoshone Indians v. United States, 324 U.S. 335, decided March 12, 1945, argued Nov. 10 and 13, 1944) recited that the 1862 commission was told the treaty was not expected to extinguish Indian title but only to secure safe travel routes and an acknowledgment of boundaries set as far from the routes as practicable. PSL's 'decided December 1945' is wrong.
corrected_instrument_cite: Act of July 5, 1862, 12 Stat. 512, 529; Shoshone Indians v. United States, 324 U.S. 335 (1945)
notes: Same case held the 1863 treaties did not recognize Shoshone title, so no compensation for the aboriginal claim on that basis. The case was brought by the Northwestern Bands, not the Eastern Shoshone.

source_title: Pacific Railway Act, July 1, 1862
source_quote: between the south margin of the valley of the Republican River and the north margin of the valley of the Platte River
corrected_summary: The 1862 Pacific Railway Act chartered a central route from the 100th meridian in Nebraska Territory west to Nevada, not a 32nd parallel route, and directed the United States to extinguish Indian titles to lands needed for the right of way and grants 'as rapidly as may be'. The link between these acts and the need for the 1863 treaty is the PSL author's argument.
corrected_instrument_cite: 12 Stat. 489 (Pacific Railway Act); 12 Stat. 392 (Homestead Act); 12 Stat. 503 (Morrill Act)
notes: PSL p.103 says the Act 'designated the 32nd parallel'; contradicted by the Act text. Act sec. 2: 'shall extinguish as rapidly as may be the Indian titles to all lands falling under the operation of this act'. The 1863 treaty Art. 3 did consent to a railway.

source_title: PSL TREC 2024 report (Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
source_quote: Doty, Lincoln, Young and Connor were all instrumental and I feel conspired together to force the 1863 signing of the treaty at Fort Bridger with all of the Shoshone bands.
corrected_summary: Shoshone historian Darren Parry (Northwestern Band) says he feels Doty, Lincoln, Brigham Young and Connor conspired to force the 1863 treaties. This is his interpretation, quoted in the PSL report; it is not established by documents checked here.
notes: Interpretive claim; characterization is Darren Parry's. Primary fact checked: the Box Elder treaty of July 30, 1863 was negotiated by Brig. Gen. P. Edward Connor and James Duane Doty (Kappler II), six months after Bear River. Exclude the 'Doty wanted Shoshone moved to Minnesota in 1841' claim from the map.

source_title: PSL TREC 2024 report (Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
source_quote: Brigham Young took control of Shoshone land, not with a treaty but through a massacre, and over 100 Mormon families moved into the area.
notes: Author's interpretation; Bear River (Jan. 29, 1863) was carried out by Connor's California Volunteers, not by Young. 'Chief Pagunapin Smithfield' name not verified. Settle with Cache Valley settlement records and Madsen, The Shoshoni Frontier and the Bear River Massacre (1985).

source_title: PSL TREC 2024 report (Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
source_quote: On May 21, 1868 (nearly two months before the Eastern Shoshone signed the 1868 Treaty) a contract was signed by Brigham Young
notes: Not checked against the Union Pacific contract or Young papers. Note 1863 Fort Bridger Art. 3 already consented to a railway 'through any portion of the country claimed by them', so the contract did not precede Shoshone consent to a railroad.

source_title: Treaty with the Eastern Shoshoni, July 2, 1863 (Kappler II)
source_quote: on the east, by the Wind River mountains, Peenahpah river, the north fork of Platte or Koo-chin-agah, and the north Park or Buffalo House;
corrected_instrument_cite: Treaty with the Eastern Shoshoni, July 2, 1863, 18 Stat. 685; Kappler II 848 (1904 ed.)
notes: Art. 4 opens 'the boundaries of the Shoshonee country, as defined and described by said nation': it records the Shoshone description and is not a US grant. Supreme Court (324 U.S. 335) held the 1863 Shoshone treaties did not recognize title. Kappler sidenote: ratified with amendment March 7, 1864; proclaimed June 7, 1869 (OCR partly garbled). Royce 520 is the 1868 relinquishment area; the 1863 boundaries are not a Royce cession.

source_title: Treaty with the Eastern Shoshoni, July 2, 1863 (Kappler II)
source_quote: it is stipulated by said nation that said railway, or its branches, may be located, constructed, and operated, without molestation from them, through any portion of the country claimed by them.
notes: Art. 3 also: telegraph and overland stage lines 'having been established and operated' may continue. Retroactive acceptance of prior use is in the text. 'Cover for prior unconsented use' is the PSL author's characterization.

source_title: Treaty with the Eastern Shoshoni, July 2, 1863 (Kappler II)
source_quote: annually for the term of twenty years, the sum of ten thousand dollars, in such articles as the Presi¬ dent of the United States may deem suitable
corrected_summary: Art. 5 promised $10,000 a year for 20 years in articles the President chose, accepted 'as a full compensation and equivalent for the loss of game, and the rights and privileges hereby conceded'. Art. 6 acknowledged $6,000 in provisions and clothing already received as presents. Claims about failed appropriations and delays are the author's and were not checked against appropriation acts.
notes: Book says compensation covered loss of game only; the text also covers 'the rights and privileges hereby conceded' (routes, posts, telegraph, railway). Delivery failures unverified; check Indian appropriation acts 1864-1868.

source_title: Shoshone Indians v. United States; Treaty with the Eastern Shoshoni, July 2, 1863 (Kappler II)
source_quote: an additional article was added to each and, except for one treaty not further involved here, accepted by the Indians.
notes: Art. 7 text confirmed in Kappler II. Supreme Court confirms it was a Senate-added article accepted by the Indians. Kappler sidenote shows ratification with amendment March 7, 1864 and proclamation June 7, 1869 (not 1875 as the round 1 note guessed).

source_title: PSL TREC 2024 report (Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
source_quote: Some identified more land in Colorado than that identified by Doty’s map.
notes: Map images not in text. Settle with the Doty 1859/1863 map in the Senate treaty file (NARA RG 46 / RG 11 ratified treaty file for July 2, 1863), O. Stewart 1957 map, and the Robertson 2023 overlay.

source_title: Treaty of Fort Laramie 1851, Art. 5 (Kappler II); Treaty with the Eastern Band Shoshoni and Bannock, July 3, 1868
source_cite: Kappler II 594 (1904 ed.), Art. 5; 15 Stat. 673, Art. II
source_quote: thence along the main range of the Black Hills and Wind River Mountains to the head- waters of the Yellowstone River
corrected_summary: The 1851 Fort Laramie treaty described Crow territory as running along the Wind River Mountains (it recognized, rather than granted, Crow country). The 1863 Fort Bridger treaty recorded Shoshone-described country but granted nothing; it was the 1868 Fort Bridger treaty that set apart the Wind River reservation for the Shoshone, with a separate future reservation for the Bannock. The Washakie and Big Robber duel at Crowheart Butte is tradition.
notes: Battle and duel details are oral tradition; Crowheart Butte closure to climbers not checked.

source_title: Commissioner Wm. P. Dole to Supt. O.H. Irish, March 28, 1865, in Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs 1865
source_quote: inasmuch as it has not been the policy of government to acknowledge the full title of these Indians to the lands claimed by them
corrected_summary: On March 28, 1865 Commissioner Dole told Superintendent Irish that, because the government's policy had not been to acknowledge the full title of the Utah Indians to the lands they claimed, treaties should have them relinquish the right of occupancy within defined boundaries and move to reserved lands. Dole did not say the government had never accepted Indian title to any land in Utah.
notes: Letter followed the Act of Feb. 23, 1865 'to extinguish the Indian title to lands in the Territory of Utah' (13 Stat. 432). Signed WILLIAM P. DOLE, Commissioner.

source_title: Treaty with the Eastern Band Shoshoni and Bannock, July 3, 1868
source_quote: commencing at the mouth of Owl creek and running due south to the crest of the divide between the Sweetwater and Papo Agie rivers
corrected_instrument_cite: 15 Stat. 673 (concluded July 3, 1868; ratification advised Feb. 16, 1869; proclaimed Feb. 24, 1869); Kappler II 1020 (1904 ed.)
notes: Art. II: 'set apart for the absolute and undisturbed use and occupation of the Shoshonee Indians herein named, and for such other friendly tribes or individual Indians as from time to time they may be willing, with the consent of the United States, to admit'. Bannock clause ('Port neuf' and 'Kansas Prairie') confirmed. Royce 520 = relinquished territory; 539 = part later ceded 1872; 540 = remainder. Signed by 8 Shoshone and 6 Bannock.

source_title: PSL TREC 2024 report (Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
source_quote: the over 40 million acres of ground taken from the Eastern Shoshone was not adequately compensated for in the 1868 Treaty.
corrected_summary: The PSL author argues the Eastern Shoshone relinquishment in 1868 was not adequately compensated. The acreage (over 40 million) and dollar valuations are the author's rough estimates and should not be mapped as figures. The 1868 treaty Art. II relinquishment is general and does not mention Colorado.
notes: No primary source checked gives a 40 million acre figure for Eastern Shoshone country; the Supreme Court (324 U.S. 335, citing Ct. Cl.) gives over 80 million acres for all Shoshone in five states. Telegraph, stage and railway uses were consented to in 1863 Art. 3 for the 1863 annuity, so 'no compensation ever' overstates.

source_title: PSL TREC 2024 report (Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
source_quote: At least one agent on the Wind River Reservation was removed for taking bribes to assign better lands to non-Indians during the allotment sale and distri- bution period in 1910.
notes: Author impressions; nothing cited. The cite 'Court of Claims No. H-129 (decided Dec 2, 1938)' could not be matched; 304 U.S. 111 shows the valuation case below was 85 Ct. Cls. 331, and the docket H-219 appears in PSL elsewhere. Winnemucca quote concerns Western Shoshone/Paiute, not Eastern Shoshone. Settle bribery claim with Wind River agency records or ARCIA 1910-1911.

source_title: Treaty with the Eastern Band Shoshoni and Bannock, July 3, 1868
source_quote: unless executed and signed by at least a majority of all the adult male Indians occupying or inter- ested in the same
notes: Majority rule (not three-fourths, as in the 1868 Ute treaty). Signers: 8 Shoshone and 6 Bannock by mark (15 Stat. 677). The 1863 treaty has no cession-consent clause, correct.

source_title: Act of Dec. 15, 1874 confirming Brunot agreement of Sept. 26, 1872 (Kappler I); Shoshone Tribe v. United States
source_quote: previous to and since the date of said treaty, mines have been discovered, and citizens of the United States have made improvements within the limits of said reservation
corrected_summary: The 1872 Brunot agreement, confirmed Dec. 15, 1874, ceded the southern part of the 1868 reservation (700,642 acres per the Supreme Court, about 23 percent of the 3,047,730-acre 1868 reservation, so about a quarter, not 'nearly a third') after miners and settlers had already moved in, as the agreement's own preamble admits. Payment was $25,000 in stock cattle over five years plus a $500 yearly salary to Washakie for five years ($27,500). The ICC (Docket 63, Aug. 20, 1954, as quoted in PSL) valued the land at $0.80 an acre ($560,513.60) and found the consideration unconscionable.
corrected_instrument_cite: 18 Stat. 291 (Act of Dec. 15, 1874, ch. 2); ICC Docket No. 63
notes: 'Nearly one-third' comes from a Jackson Hole Historical Society note quoted in PSL, not a primary source. Cross-check: $560,513.60 / $0.80 = 700,642 acres, matching 299 U.S. 487. Art. III bound the US 'not to permit the intrusion of any white persons' until the line was surveyed. Agreement recites consent of 'a majority of all the adult male Indians'. ICC decision text not reached (okstate down); quote is via PSL.

source_title: United States v. Shoshone Tribe of Indians
source_quote: there were allotted to members of the tribes 245,058 acres
corrected_summary: Allotment carved parts of the Wind River reservation into individual parcels; the Supreme Court records 245,058 acres allotted to tribal members from 1907 to 1919. The opening of 'surplus' land to non-Native homesteaders came through the 1904 agreement ratified by the Act of March 3, 1905 (33 Stat. 1016), under which the US acted as trustee to sell the land, not through the Dawes Act itself or a sale to the government.
corrected_instrument_cite: 24 Stat. 388 (General Allotment Act); 33 Stat. 1016 (Act of March 3, 1905)
notes: Washakie 'God damn a potato!' quote is book only (secondary).

source_title: Act of June 7, 1897, ch. 3, sec. 12 (Agreement with Shoshone and Arapahoe, April 21, 1896)
source_quote: Beginning at the northeastern corner of the said reservation, where Owl Creek empties into the Big Horn River; thence south ten miles, following the eastern boundary of the reservation; thence due west ten miles
notes: Sec. 12: the amended agreement 'shall be binding upon said Indians when they shall in the usual manner agree to the amendment herein made thereto'. Royce area for the 1896 cession not found in the atlas crosswalk; check Royce Wyoming plate.

source_title: Shoshone Tribe of Indians v. United States
source_quote: agreed that they might remain for a short time to rest their horses and themselves
notes: Resolves the contradiction inside PSL. The Supreme Court found the Commissioner wrongly assumed Shoshone consent from a misread Oct. 1877 telegram, ignored warnings 'that consent had been refused', and brought the Arapaho under military escort on March 18, 1878 (not 19; Ct. Cl. used March 19 as the taking date). Washakie agreed only to a short rest; Shoshone protests were ignored. Stamm's 'only with the consent of the Shoshones' (PSL p.132) should not be mapped. 1868 Art. II allowed other tribes only 'with the consent of the United States' and of the Shoshone ('they may be willing').

source_title: PSL TREC 2024 report (Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
source_quote: the govern- ment made the Arapahos equal partners to the Shoshones in the rights to claim the reservation
notes: Hank Stamm's characterization. Primary text partly supports it: the 1896 agreement was made with 'the Shoshone and Arapahoe tribes' jointly and $60,000 was paid to both (30 Stat. 94). But Stamm's statement in the same passage that the Arapaho came in 1878 'only with the consent of the Shoshones' is contradicted by 299 U.S. 476, 487. The Supreme Court says the Commissioner treated the tribes as equal beneficiaries from 1878 on, not first in 1896.

source_title: Act of June 7, 1897, ch. 3, sec. 12
source_quote: the sum of sixty thousand dollars, to be expended for the benefit of the said Indians in the manner hereinafter described.
notes: Art. III: $10,000 per capita or stock cattle; $50,000 in five annual installments for 'civilization, industrial education, and subsistence' at the Secretary's discretion. Signatures of Washakie, Sharp Nose and 271 others (273). The reason given for ceding (Big Horn Basin game destroyed by ranches from 1879) is book only (Stamm).

source_title: Act of June 7, 1897, ch. 3, sec. 12
source_quote: the foregoing names, though in some cases duplicates, in every instance represents different individuals.
notes: Acting agent Capt. Richard H. Wilson, 8th Infantry, certified the 273 'constitute a majority of all male Indians over eighteen (18) years of age, belonging on the Shoshone Reservation': a combined count, no per-tribe majority stated. Interpretation as a legitimacy problem is round 1's, not a source's.

source_title: Act of June 7, 1897, ch. 3, sec. 12
source_quote: one mile square at and about the principal hot spring thereon contained, is hereby ceded, granted, relinquished, and conveyed unto the State of Wyoming
notes: Act made the agreement binding 'when they shall in the usual manner agree to the amendment herein made thereto'; tribal assent to the amendment not shown in this text (a sidenote cross-references 30 Stat. 581). Rest declared public lands open 'only under the homestead and town-site laws'.

source_title: Act of March 3, 1905, ch. 1452 (Agreement of April 21, 1904)
source_quote: is four hundred and eighty-four (484), of whom two hundred and eighty-two (282) have signed the foregoing agreement.
notes: Statute confirms 282 of 484 adult males signed, consistent with PSL's 202 of 247 Shoshone plus 80 of 237 Arapaho. Per-tribe split and Lone Bear's departure are book only (WyoHistory.org). Supreme Court: 1,480,000 acres ceded 'to be held by it in trust' (304 U.S. 111).

source_title: Act of March 3, 1905, ch. 1452
source_quote: Articles II, III, and IX, which are amended and modified as follows
notes: Lone Bear's telegram text is book only, but the statute shows Congress did change the signed agreement: it amended Arts. II, III and IX, and the amended Art. IX dropped the signed promise that the US would buy sections 16 and 36 in each township. So the protest that the ratified version differed from what was signed is supported by the statute itself.

source_title: Act of March 3, 1905, ch. 1452, sec. 2
source_quote: June fifteenth, nineteen hundred and six
corrected_summary: The 1905 Act set the opening of the ceded lands for June 15, 1906 by presidential proclamation. Revenue figures ($2.2 million projected, about $500,000 received), the elders' 1906 protest and the 1909/1914 sale percentages are from the WyoHistory.org article quoted in PSL and were not checked against primary records.
corrected_instrument_cite: 33 Stat. 1016, sec. 2; Presidential proclamation of 1906 (not checked)
notes: Settle sale figures with Commissioner of Indian Affairs annual reports 1909 and 1914.

source_title: PSL TREC 2024 report (Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
source_quote: Construction was financed by money that Mondell managed to have allocated to it that year from Congress’ annual appro- priations meant for Indian reservations.
notes: Primary support for the promise only: 33 Stat. 1016 Art. IV earmarked sale proceeds for 'an irrigation system within the diminished reservation for the irrigation of the lands of the said Indians'. The 1919 Riverton Project financing claim needs the 1919 Indian or reclamation appropriation act.

source_title: Wyoming v. EPA, Nos. 14-9512, 14-9514 (10th Cir. 2017) (amended opinion Nov. 7, 2017)
source_quote: approximately seventy-five percent of the land affected by the 1905 Act is held in trust by the United States
notes: Majority: 'by its 1905 legislation, Congress evinced a clear intent to diminish the Reservation'. Interior Solicitor (2011) and EPA had concluded the 1905 Act did not change the 1868 boundaries (confirmed). In the amended opinion the 75 percent trust figure appears in the majority; Lucero, J. dissented. The holding concerns reservation boundary (Indian country) status, not land ownership; PSL's 'belongs to the State of Wyoming' overstates. Cert. denial date not checked.

source_title: Shoshone Tribe of Indians v. United States
source_quote: gress the jurisdictional Act of March 3, 1927, under which they
corrected_summary: Congress allowed the Shoshone to sue by the jurisdictional Act of March 3, 1927 (ch. 302), not 1928. On Jan. 4, 1937 the Supreme Court held that putting the Arapaho on the Shoshone reservation was a taking of a Shoshone property interest requiring just compensation, with interest. The settlement terms requiring Shoshone recognition of Arapaho residence, and the renaming to 'Wind River', are book only.
notes: Syllabus: 'The guardianship of the United States ... does not enable the Government to require a tribe to which an exclusive right of occupancy has been pledged by treaty, to share it with another tribe without just compensation.'

source_title: United States v. Shoshone Tribe of Indians
source_quote: Minerals and standing timber are constituent elements of the land
corrected_instrument_cite: Shoshone Tribe v. United States, 85 Ct. Cls. 331; affirmed, 304 U.S. 111 (1938)
notes: Decided April 25, 1938, Butler, J. Court quotes Ct. Cl. finding: one-half interest of 2,343,540 acres taken March 19, 1878 worth $1,581,889.50, 'That is $1.35 per acre for 1,171,770 acres'. Row quote wording slightly differs from the opinion; use the exact wording above.

source_title: Act of July 27, 1939, ch. 387
source_quote: Not to exceed $1,000,000 of said judgment fund
corrected_summary: The Act of July 27, 1939 credited $2,450 to each enrolled Shoshone member: $100 available at once, $1,350 per adult (or $500 per minor) for land, homes, livestock and similar purposes, and the remainder under Interior rules (minors' shares held until age 18). Up to $1,000,000 of the judgment fund could buy land. The 'about $4.2 million' net figure is book only.
notes: Judgment fund arose from the Act of June 25, 1938 (52 Stat. 1114, 1156). 10th Cir. (Wyoming v. EPA) notes the 1939 Act also directed restoration of unsold 1905 ceded lands to tribal ownership (53 Stat. 1128, 1129).

source_title: Act of Dec. 15, 1874, ch. 2 (Kappler I)
source_quote: An Act to confirm an agreement made with the Shoshone Indians (eastern band ) for the purchase of the south part of their reservation
notes: Pointer row. Title and date confirmed. Library file STAT-18-291 is the wrong document (Revised Statutes title XVII), do not cite it; the act is in 18 Stat. pt. 3, p. 291. Fed. Cir. 2004 quote not checked.

source_title: ICC, Shoshone Tribe of Indians of the Wind River Reservation v. United States, Docket No. 63 (Aug. 20, 1954)
notes: Pointer row. ICC text not reached (okstate.edu down). PSL p. 127 quotes findings: Brunot lands worth $0.80/acre, $560,513.60; $27,500 unconscionable. Acreage implied (700,642) matches 299 U.S. 487. Settle with the ICC decision text (Indian Claims Commission Decisions vol. 2 or 3).

source_quote: Only about 10 percent of the Reservation is owned by non-Indians.
notes: Federal Circuit opinion not reached (courtlistener blocked). Settle with Shoshone Indian Tribe of the Wind River Reservation v. United States, 364 F.3d 1339 (Fed. Cir. 2004).

source_quote: rejected it by a vote of 339 for and 469 against on June 15, 1935.
notes: Vote not checked. Settle with Haas, Ten Years of Tribal Government Under I.R.A. (1947), table of IRA votes.

source_title: Wyoming v. United States
source_quote: 753 P. 2d 76, affirmed by an equally divided Court.
corrected_summary: Big Horn I (753 P.2d 76, Wyo. 1988) recognized the tribes' 1868 reserved (Winters) water right; the US Supreme Court affirmed by an equally divided Court in Wyoming v. United States, 492 U.S. 406 (1989) (decided June 26, 1989). The Big Horn III ruling against instream use is 835 P.2d 273 (Wyo. 1992). PSL's '49 U.S. 406' is a typo.
corrected_instrument_cite: 753 P.2d 76 (Wyo. 1988), aff'd by an equally divided Court, 492 U.S. 406 (1989); 835 P.2d 273 (Wyo. 1992)
notes: 835 P.2d 273 not fetched; its holding and the 'futures' water status are book only. 'Infringe and control' is the author's characterization.

source_title: Herrera v. Wyoming
source_quote: The Crow Tribe’s hunting rights under the 1868 Treaty did not expire upon Wyoming’s statehood.
corrected_summary: The Supreme Court held the Crow Tribe's 1868 treaty hunting right did not expire at Wyoming statehood and vacated and remanded. PSL's phrase 'treaty rights are not extinguished at statehood' paraphrases the holding. The 2023 dismissal and HB 83 history are book only.
notes: 587 U.S. 329 is from general knowledge, not checked; slip opinion No. 17-532 is in the library.

source_title: Northwestern Band of the Shoshone Nation v. Wooten, No. 22-35140 (9th Cir. Oct. 17, 2023)
source_quote: plainly do not condition exercise of the reserved hunting right on the Northwestern Band relocating to a reservation.
corrected_instrument_cite: Northwestern Band of the Shoshone Nation v. Wooten, No. 22-35140 (9th Cir. 2023)
notes: Reversed and remanded. The 80 million acre 'time immemorial' recital is the Ninth Circuit quoting Northwestern Bands v. United States, 95 Ct. Cl. 642, 644 (1942). Case came up from D. Idaho; PSL's 'filed in the Ninth Circuit' is wrong.

Note Art. 4 boundaries are those 'defined and described by said nation'; a wider Shoshone-described country does not by itself establish unceded title, because 1868 Art. II relinquished all territory outside the reservation.

source_quote: relinquish all of their claim, right, title, and interest in and to any and all of their lands within the territory of the United States, wherever situated, excepting that which is included within the following boundaries
corrected_summary: The 1863 treaty ceded all Tabeguache-claimed lands outside the reserve described in Art. II. Since the recital of Tabeguache country ran along the base of the Rockies from the 37th to the 41st parallel and included North and Middle Park, the cession took the Front Range and parks east of the Continental Divide and Middle Park, including Pikes Peak (Tava). The treaty does not name Tava or Pikes Peak; that identification and its sacred meaning come from PSL.
notes: Wording 'all Rocky Mountain land east of the Continental Divide' is a reasonable reading of recital plus cession within the claimed area, not treaty language.

The Senate struck the Sandy Creek and Rio Grande segment (the quoted words) and changed 'Arkansas' to 'Gunnison's Fork of the Great Colorado', so the reserve as ratified excluded the San Luis Valley. In the Statutes at Large the Tabeguache label sits beside the group led by Ou-ray and the Mouache label beside the group led by Ka-ni-ache, so PSL's reversal is a transcription error. The claim that no Capote signed the original is doubtful: Capote assent signer Ba-bu-zat appears to be original signer Pa-bu-sat.

corrected_summary: After the 1879 Meeker and Milk Creek fighting, Congress ratified the 1880 Ute agreement with amendments: only the White River Utes' share (except removal costs) was withheld until the guilty parties surrendered or were accounted for, and annual payments to Meeker victims and relatives were charged to the White River share. The Supreme Court (330 U.S. 169) described the removal as part of the punishment. The Uncompahgre were also removed, to Utah.
